summary: Deep dive on on-prem air-gapped deployment: artifact delivery process, offline licensing and driver packaging, GPU driver/kernel compatibility, runtime tuning (KV cache, batching, quantization). transcript: 00:00 Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, we'll run through the on-prem, airgap deep dive today. Jonah and Hannah are with me from solutions engineering.
00:12 Priya Singh: Hi, thanks, we've got about an hour, so main goals are: offline install story, driver licensing, and performance tuning for low-latency inference in our private data center.

00:25 Jonah Li: Great, quick agenda — artifact delivery options, offline license flow, GPU driver notes, then runtime knobs: KV cache behavior, batching, quantization tradeoffs, and then Q&A and next steps.
00:40 Marco Ruiz: Quick note, we're fully air-gapped, no outbound internet from inference cluster; we can do offline file transfer via secure USB or internal jump host but no external pki calls.

00:51 Hannah O'Neill: Perfect, that's a common setup. We'll outline both a completely offline artifact bundle and an optional license-server approach that runs in your mgmt network if you can allow one-way comms.
01:05 Sophie Turner: Also want to confirm SOC2/ISO implications — we need audit logs for model usage and license checks; are those produced locally or sent to Redwood?

01:18 Maya Patel: For Private we support local audit logs. The offline licensing flow writes license tokens and audit events locally. If you opt for the managed license server you can keep logs internal to your VPC; nothing is sent back by default.
01:32 Priya Singh: Ok, good. Marco, can you run us through current infra?

01:36 Marco Ruiz: Sure — we have racks with H100s (80GB) on Rocky Linux 9, currently kernel 5.15, using containerd runtime. We'll need specific NVIDIA driver versions and matching CUDA; procurement may take weeks for signed offline artifacts though.

01:52 Jonah Li: Noted — for H100 we'd recommend NVIDIA driver 535.x series and CUDA 12.2 roughly; but exact kernel-module compatibility matters. We'll give you a driver checklist with kernel ABI checks and DKMS steps — that usually reduces surprises.
02:08 Marco Ruiz: Are we able to use Redwood-provided optimized kernels, or do we rely on stock NVIDIA packages?

02:14 Hannah O'Neill: The runtime can use stock NVIDIA drivers; for optimized kernels we ship optional kernel modules and tuned libs in the artifact bundle. In air-gapped installs customers often prefer pre-bundled libs that match their exact kernel — we provide checksums and signatures for verification.
02:30 Priya Singh: How do you deliver artifacts? physically or via internal transfer?

02:35 Maya Patel: We support both. Typical flow: we produce a signed tarball (runtime, model weights, drivers if allowed) plus a license file. You can fetch via a secure SFTP from a temporary bridge host, or we can ship an encrypted USB with transfer instructions. All artifacts are SHA256-signed and we provide PGP signatures.
02:52 Sophie Turner: For compliance, we need to see the signing certs and an offline verification script. Can you provide those?
02:57 Maya Patel: Yes, we'll include the verification script and PGP public key. That's part of the checklist I'll send.
03:08 Marco Ruiz: On the license side, what's the offline licensing model? file-based? server?

03:12 Jonah Li: Two options: a file-based license (signed token installed on host) or a local license server that runs in your control plane and issues ephemeral leases to inference nodes. File-based is easier for full air-gap but less flexible for rotations.
03:26 Priya Singh: Rotation is important. Can file-based licenses be rotated without internet?

03:29 Hannah O'Neill: You can rotate by installing a new token bundle via the same offline process; we support time-limited tokens and offline revocation lists that you can push during maintenance windows.
03:43 Marco Ruiz: Any HSM/KMS integrations? We use an on-prem HSM for key material — would Redwood integrate?

03:48 Maya Patel: We support pointing the private deployment at your KMS via local connectors. For fully offline HSM workflows, we can accept signed CSR material and deliver license blobs that map to your keys — we'll include integration docs.
03:59 Priya Singh: Ok. Let's get into runtime perf — our key metric is 95th percentile latency for chat endpoints, target under 120ms for short prompts.

04:08 Jonah Li: For that target on H100 with 80GB and optimized model (quantized to int8 or nf4 where supported), typical observations: single-request latency is dominated by token generation, attention kernel, and KV cache hits. If you can ensure warm KV caches and small batch sizes (1-4), you can hit low 95p latencies. We'll show numbers.

04:28 Maya Patel: Note: quantization trades off some quality for big throughput/latency gains. We can recommend quant profiles per model and workload. For QA, we usually run eval sets to ensure quality stays within acceptable regression thresholds.
04:40 Daniel Lee: What's Redwood's recommended batching strategy for a low-latency requirement?

04:44 Jonah Li: We suggest continuous micro-batching: keep batch windows short (10-20ms) and target effective batch sizes 2-8 depending on traffic burstiness. For chat with low concurrency, batch of 2-4 often gives best latency/cost balance. For high throughput, you can increase to 16-32 but 95p latency increases.
04:59 Marco Ruiz: You mentioned KV cache — how does prefix caching interact with multiple tenant workloads?

05:04 Hannah O'Neill: KV caching stores previous key-value states for sequences to avoid recomputing prefixes. In multi-tenant setups you can either have per-tenant cache partitions or a shared cache with TTLs. Per-tenant avoids cross-tenant leakage and simplifies compliance, but uses more memory.
05:18 Priya Singh: Memory footprint is a concern. Our instance density target is 4 models per GPU on average.

05:24 Jonah Li: With H100 80GB and int8 quant workloads you can often host multiple model variants; however KV cache memory scales with sequence length and number of concurrent sessions. We can provide a sizing spreadsheet for your target concurrency and sequence length distribution.
05:36 Marco Ruiz: Can you share a sample sizing calc?
05:39 Jonah Li: Yes I'll attach a calc; it will show tokens-per-session, KV bytes per token, and resulting GPU memory overhead. We'll include conservative and aggressive profiles.
05:51 Sophie Turner: On quantization — are you doing post-training quant only, or do you recommend QAT for critical models?

05:56 Hannah O'Neill: Generally we start with PTQ (post-training quant) using per-channel symmetric schemes like nf4 or int8 where supported. If you have strict quality requirements, we can recommend QAT or selective layers in fp16. We'll show sample eval diffs.
06:10 Priya Singh: Back to drivers — we need an offline installer for NVIDIA drivers and CUDA libs; what packaging do you provide?

06:16 Maya Patel: We provide OS-specific packages: rpm/deb bundles plus a container-friendly lib bundle for containerd/runc. For kernel module mismatches we include DKMS sources and instructions. Everything is hashed and signed.
06:28 Marco Ruiz: Are pre-built optimized CUDA kernels included or do we compile locally?

06:31 Jonah Li: We ship prebuilt optimized kernels for common kernels and fallback sources to compile. If your kernel is non-standard we'll provide build instructions and a compile script that runs locally; that's slower but predictable.
06:43 Sophie Turner: In terms of support SLAs for offline installs, what's Redwood's policy?

06:47 Maya Patel: For Private customers we offer enterprise support tiers with defined RTOs for offline installs. We also provide runbooks and a dedicated solutions engineer during the initial rollout window.
06:56 Priya Singh: Great. Any gotchas around container runtimes? We use containerd and gVisor on some workloads.

07:03 Jonah Li: gVisor can introduce additional syscalls cost; for performance you'd prefer minimal sandboxing on inference nodes. Containerd is fine; ensure NVIDIA container toolkit is installed and matches driver/CUDA versions.
07:15 Marco Ruiz: About benchmarking — what exact workloads should we run to validate latency/throughput?

07:20 Hannah O'Neill: We'll provide a bench harness: synthetic token-level latency runs, realistic chat replay (from your logs if permitted), and mixed concurrency tests. The harness will output p50/p90/p95 latencies and throughput at target batch sizes and sequence lengths.
07:33 Priya Singh: We'll want to run both short prompt (<=64 tokens) and long conversation (>=512 tokens) profiles.
07:38 Jonah Li: Exactly — short prompts are more sensitive to kernel latency and batching. Long sequences stress KV cache and memory; quantization can provide big wins there.
07:47 Marco Ruiz: For artifact transfer, can you provide a checklist for us to validate before install? checksums, pgp, driver version, kernel headers, etc.

07:55 Maya Patel: Yes checklist will include: host kernel version, glibc version, container runtime version, driver version, cuda version, GPU firmware, available disk space, SELinux/AppArmor considerations, and offline license steps. We'll include commands to verify (uname -r, modinfo nvidia, nvidia-smi outputs) in the bundle.
08:10 Sophie Turner: We need a sample of the audit logs format so our security team can pre-validate ingestion into SIEM.
08:15 Maya Patel: We'll include a sample audit log and field mapping for Splunk/ELK in the docs.
08:21 Priya Singh: Let's talk about fallback/resilience: if a node fails mid-conversation, how do you ensure statelessness or state recovery?

08:27 Jonah Li: For chat we recommend externalized KV persistence for long-lived sessions: store the KV blob in a secure object store (internal S3) with appropriate encryption. If a node fails, the new node can reload the KV state. There's a tradeoff in reload latency — prefetched hot prefixes reduce that.
08:42 Marco Ruiz: That implies network access to internal object store from inference nodes; we can allow that in our private network.
08:47 Hannah O'Neill: Good — we'll document the recommended pattern and TTLs for cache objects.
08:54 Priya Singh: Any specific quant profiles you recommend for conversational models?

08:58 Jonah Li: nf4 is a great starting point on many open models; int8 can yield further memory/throughput improvements but needs evals. We'll include precomputed quant profiles for the models we're recommending.
09:09 Marco Ruiz: For the initial pilot, we want minimal operational work: file-based license, prebuilt drivers, one model variant (nf4), and bench harness run. Feels doable.
09:19 Maya Patel: Sounds like a reasonable pilot. Action items recap coming in the notes; today we lock on the pilot scope and timeline.
09:26 Priya Singh: Timeline — procurement needs two weeks for signed NDA and artifact acceptance. Can you accommodate a mid-August install?
09:32 Maya Patel: Yes, we can target August 18-20 for artifact transfer and install if paperwork is cleared. We'll put provisional slots on the calendar.
09:40 Sophie Turner: A couple more quick Qs: are offline driver licenses (like NVIDIA GRID style) needed?
09:45 Jonah Li: Usually no — we rely on standard NVIDIA drivers; GRID licensing is separate and would be handled by your procurement if you need vGPU licenses. We'll call that out in the checklist.
09:56 Marco Ruiz: Any special kernel build flags we should watch for?
09:59 Hannah O'Neill: Avoid custom preemption patches; standard distro kernels are easiest. We'll include dkms config suggestions and a fallback prebuilt kernel module if needed.
10:09 Priya Singh: Awesome. Can we get a one-page runbook showing the install flow?
10:13 Maya Patel: Yes — we'll attach a 1-page runbook to the follow-up email along with the checklist and bench harness.
10:21 Maya Patel: Ok let's do a quick recap of next steps and owners — Maya send docs, Jonah share benchmarks, Marco supply infra details and confirm dates, Priya will coordinate procurement.
10:33 Priya Singh: Thanks everyone. That was helpful — we'll review the docs and come back with any compliance questions.
10:39 Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up with artifacts and proposed install slots. End of call.
10:46 [call ends]
